title: High-Dimensional Signal Processing using Classical-Quantum Machine Learning Pipelines with the TensorFlow Stack, Cirq-NISQ, and Vertica
journal_or_venue: 2022 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)
abstract_summary: The paper addresses ground-truth and class-imbalance challenges in high-dimensional signal data by generating statistically accurate synthetic data using an entangled unsupervised Quantum Generative Adversarial Network (uQGAN) implemented with parameterized Cirq NISQ circuits and TensorFlow Quantum. The synthetic data is then used to train a classical ResNet18-based CNN on GPUs, and the validated model (or its feature map) is exported to a Vertica production cluster for high-speed in-database inference and model stacking; the approach also proposes incorporating a NISQ noise model to improve quantum error robustness.
methodology_description: The authors propose a hybrid classical-quantum pipeline to generate synthetic high-dimensional signal data (HDSD) with an entangled unsupervised Quantum Generative Adversarial Network (uQGAN) built using Cirq and TensorFlow Quantum (TFQ). Classical image data (Galaxy Zoo) is first balanced, converted to greyscale, resized to 4x4, and converted into binary strings (basis encoding) to prepare for QRAM-style quantum state loading. Each pixel is mapped to a qubit, and shallow parametrized Cirq NISQ circuits approximate a QRAM superposition. An entangled uQGAN consisting of two parameterized quantum circuits — a quantum generator (QGEN) and a quantum discriminator (QDIS) — is trained adversarially; the QGEN emits synthetic quantum data (entangled with real samples) and the QDIS attempts to distinguish real vs. synthetic. Variables are shared between QGEN and QDIS through a TFQ/Keras layer. To improve robustness to NISQ errors, the authors plan a custom noise model including bit-flip, phase-flip, and combined bit-and-phase-flip errors to force the QGEN to model decoherence effects and improve effective QEC. The resulting synthetic dataset (entangled outputs from the QDIS) becomes a new ‘‘ground truth’’ dataset which is exported to classical TensorFlow/Keras for training a classical CNN (pretrained ResNet18 backbone). The trained TF model is then exported into a Vertica analytics cluster for either direct TF-model inference at ingest or a model-stacking approach where TF-derived feature maps feed VerticaML classifiers/regressors/clustering models for high-speed, in-database inference.
algorithms_used: Basis encoding / QRAM approximation via shallow circuits
experimental_setup: Cirq-based NISQ circuits prepared and executed via TensorFlow Quantum; classical preprocessing on CPU/GPU (TensorFlow/Keras); target quantum execution on a Google NISQ system / QPU (Cirq TFQ integration). Dataset reduced to 1,000 images resized to 4x4 (16 pixels/qubits) to accommodate current NISQ limitations. Plans to include a custom quantum noise model (bit-flip, phase-flip, bit-and-phase-flip).

results_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid classical–quantum pipeline for high-dimensional signal processing: convert and binary-encode classical data for quantum state preparation, train an entangled unsupervised QGAN (implemented in Cirq/TFQ) to produce synthetic signal data, combine entangled real and synthetic outputs at the quantum discriminator to form a new labelled/ground-truth dataset, and then train a classical TF-Keras CNN (ResNet18) on the synthetic data. The validated TensorFlow model is intended to be exported to a Vertica production cluster for either direct TF inference or for model-stacking via VerticaML to enable real-time inference at data ingest. The manuscript describes dataset preparation and the uQGAN architecture and workflow, but provides no empirical performance metrics for the end-to-end pipeline; several aspects (noise-model integration, classical training, final validation, and production deployment) are noted as in-progress or future work.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper asserts (citing prior literature) that entangled uQGANs can achieve an exponential advantage over classical GANs for generating high-quality synthetic data, but it does not present empirical results within this work to demonstrate that advantage; the claim is therefore presented as prospective/theoretical rather than experimentally validated here.
limitations: NISQ systems are error-prone and exhibit decoherence, inhibiting practical quantum uses (author-stated).
Quantum RAM (QRAM) loading is a limiting factor for classical-to-quantum data conversion and affects scalability (author-stated).

Dataset had to be drastically downsampled and reduced (to 1,000 images resized to 4x4) to accommodate current QPU processing capabilities, limiting fidelity and realism of experiments (author-stated).

Because of the very large number of classical datapoint features, classical neural networks are expected to outperform quantum neural networks for full-resolution data — necessitating a hybrid approach (author-stated).
Key pipeline steps (classical model training, validation, and production deployment) are still in progress; no complete validation or end-to-end results are reported (author-stated).
